lines.text: So here's the shape of this whole topic: a lookup always checks the newest place a value could be first, which is exactly why a fresh, unflushed write beats an old, already-flushed one every time.

That same newest-first order means an older key costs more to find than a newer one, and a key that genuinely doesn't exist anywhere costs the most of all, because ruling it out means checking every single structure there is.
And once any one of those structures gets flushed to disk, it stops changing entirely; from that moment on, it's read from, merged with others, or eventually deleted, but never edited in place again.
